newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica rand gains from liquidation of stale longs.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica rand gains from liquidation of stale longs.

text.p: Speculators facing losses on their long dollar, short rand positions have been forced to cut their positions, helping the rand strengthen 1.5 percent over the last week, analysts said on Wednesday.

The rand firmed to its best level since August 8 on Wednesday morning when it touched 4.4950 bid against the dollar. It has gained nearly seven cents since early last week when it staged several attempts on the technically important 4.57 level.
Analysts said that players -- including hedge funds -- who had bought and held dollars in the hope that the rand's value would fall further had been forced to sell their dollars to avoid losses.

"Since the end of last week we have seen mainly offshore liquidation of long dollar positions because we were not breaking the (higher) levels," said a senior trader at one of South Africa's four major banks who declined to be quoted.
"Most of that took place between 4.55 and 4.56 and downwards," he said, noting that the liquidaton of the positions appeared to be slowing.
Doug Bate, foreign exchange manager at Standard Chartered Bank in London, said there had also been profit-taking from around the 4.57 level.

"The break of 4.59 did not materialise and we have seen a lot of people turning around positions in the rand," Bate said. "We have also seen a lot of mark/rand and sterling/rand being unwound as well."
The South African trader noted that most of the long positions being unwound were by short-term players who were likely to reposition themselves at current levels.

"The short-term players normally tend to play a range. They got squeezed out for a break at the top, but they are more than likely to reposition themselves at or just below the 4.50 level," he said. "So the downside is pretty limited."
Charles Jonker at Absa Treasury said speculators were also known to be rolling over long dollar positions in the one-week area, while hoping that the rand would continue to weaken.

"There are a couple of offshore speculators who bought the rand at specific levels and are now doing rollovers in the one-week period as they try to remain long while hoping that the rand will weaken again."

Jonker said given the currency's latest move, these positions were also likely to be squeezed, leading to further dollar sales which could take the rand to 4.48 or possibly 4.45, although he said the latter "seems a bit far off at the moment".
Bate said a "quick overshoot" to the 4.45 level was possible.
"But after (Reserve Bank Governor) Chris Stals' comments yesterday, I don't think too many people who have missed this move already will want to start buying rand at the sub-4.50 level," Bate said.

He said Stals comments on the amount the central bank had spent on trying to prop up the rand, continuing concern about the country's reserves and the fact that the bank would monitor money supply to determine the direction of domestic interest rates would stand against the rand's firming further.

"I think we might see a quick overshoot on the downside, but I think we are going to come back to the 4.50 to 4.55 range," Bate said. "I still think there will be a gradual depreciation of the rand but it will be a slow, tortuous process."
